Before the dollar moves, you need to know what it's actually buying.
Picture a company as a pizza that's been cut into slices.
Each slice is a small piece of ownership, and that slice is called a share.
The stock market is simply the place where people trade those slices.
Here's a simple example to show how slices work, with made-up numbers.
Say a pizza shop is worth one hundred dollars and is cut into one hundred slices.
Each slice is worth one dollar, so owning one slice means owning one percent.
If the shop grows to two hundred dollars, your slice is worth two dollars.
If the shop shrinks to fifty dollars, your slice is worth fifty cents.
Fifty cents is exactly why I keep my coins at home.
Now comes the part where a price tag can fool you.
Say Company A's stock costs five hundred dollars a share, and Company B's costs five dollars.
The five-hundred-dollar share looks like the bigger company, and that's the trap.
Company A is cut into only three slices, so its whole pizza is worth fifteen hundred dollars.
Company B is cut into a million slices, so its whole pizza is worth five million.
The cheap slice came from the far bigger pizza.
Price times the number of shares is called market cap, the company's market value.
Apple is cut into about fourteen and a half billion shares, which is how its value reaches trillions.

Stop one is the investing app on your phone.
Say it's Tuesday morning, and you buy one dollar of Apple.
One Apple share costs a few hundred dollars, so your dollar buys a crumb.
Many big apps sell these crumbs, and they're called fractional shares.
You place a market order, which means buy right away at the available price.
The price you saw on screen can change before your order goes through.
Your broker may also bundle your crumb with other customers' orders before it buys.
Your broker can send that order to an exchange or a market maker, or fill it itself.
I've been turned into paperwork, and nobody even said thank you.
Stop two is a kind of company most people have never heard of.
Many retail orders don't go straight to a stock exchange.
Brokers often send them to a trading firm called a market maker instead.
Picture a currency booth at the airport, with one price to buy and one to sell.
A market maker works the same way, regularly posting a buy price and a sell price.
Say it will buy Apple at three hundred fifty dollars and sell at three hundred fifty and two cents.
That two-cent gap is called the spread, and the market maker tries to earn it.
It can lose money too, because the price can move against it a minute later.
Citadel Securities says it executes about a third of all U.S. retail stock trading volume.
Market makers often pay brokers for sending them orders, which is called payment for order flow.
That's one reason many apps charge no commission on stock trades.
Your broker still has to try to get you the best available deal, considering price and how reliably the order can be filled.
Everyone on this trip gets paid except the pig, apparently.
If the market maker has the shares, it can sell them straight from its own inventory.
If it doesn't, your order can head to stop three.
Stop three is the stock exchange, the place most people picture when they hear Wall Street.

Nasdaq's main U.S. data center sits in Carteret, New Jersey.
I came all this way for Wall Street, and I got New Jersey.
An exchange works like a matchmaker that keeps two lists.

When a buyer and a seller agree on a price, the exchange matches them.
Regular trading runs from nine thirty to four, Eastern time, Monday through Friday.
Market holidays and a few early-close days are the exceptions.
Some apps let you trade earlier or later, when far fewer people are trading.
Fewer traders can mean bigger price jumps and a wider gap between buy and sell prices.
Quick check, because look at how far your dollar has already come.

Stop two was a market maker, which may sell to you from its own shelf.

Pick how much of your dollar Apple gets, all of it, half, or none.

Now comes the part that matters most, which is how one dollar turns into more dollars.
There are two main ways to make money from owning a stock.
The first is selling for more than you paid.
Here's a made-up example to show how that works.
Say Maya buys ten shares at two hundred dollars each, which costs two thousand dollars.
A year later, Jordan offers two hundred fifty dollars a share for all ten.
Maya sells and makes five hundred dollars, before taxes and any fees.
If Jordan had offered one hundred fifty dollars a share, Maya would have lost five hundred.
The second way is dividends, when a company shares part of its profits with its owners.
